catalog_quote: Le shiwa est une langue à tons. Il utilise donc les variations de la hauteur de la voix pour distinguer les ‘’mots’’. Le ton est généralement associé à un support vocalique. En shiwa, il peut être associé à des consonnes nasales utilisées comme indice de classe et à des voyelles. [...] [p.174] En shiwa, quatre tons ont une valeur distinctive : le ton haut, le ton bas, le ton montant et le ton descendant. Les tons modulés ne sont pertinents que sur les lexèmes monosyllabiques. Dans les autres cas, seuls les tons hauts et bas sont pertinents. new_statements.translation: Shiwa is a tone language. It therefore uses variations in voice pitch to distinguish 'words'. Tone is generally associated with a vocalic support; in Shiwa it can be associated with nasal consonants used as class markers and with vowels. [...] In Shiwa four tones are distinctive: high, low, rising and falling. The contour tones are relevant only on monosyllabic lexemes. [...] 1) Position: in polysyllabic lexemes the initial position is a raising position and the final position a lowering position.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Shiwa is described purely as a tone language (H, L, and rising/falling contours on monosyllables; six phonetic levels/contours across three registers). The most complete description (317-pp. thesis with a 35-page tone chapter and instrumental F0 data) has no notion of word stress or accent at all; the only positional asymmetry it reports is tonal register (lexeme-initial syllable realised on a raised register, lexeme-final on a lowered one). A shorter earlier sketch (Dougère 2007: 48-49) remarks in passing that V2/word-final stem vowels reduce or elide because they are 'dénuée d'accent … dans une position faible', implying stem-initial prominence, but no source states an accent-placement rule.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. Dougère 2007 (pp.48-49) is the only text using the word 'accent': non-initial (V2, final) mid-open vowels centralise or drop 'quand la voyelle est dénuée d'accent et donc située dans une position faible', more often in young speakers; nominal prefixes are always low-toned (Dougère p.84) and the syllabic nasal prefix bears L (Ollomo Ella p.175).
new_statements.domain_note: Ollomo Ella's tonal analysis is on the lexème (stem/word in citation form, from recorded wordlists, with Praat F0 figures); positional raising/lowering refers to lexeme-initial vs lexeme-final syllables. No phrase-level prominence discussed.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe the same variety: Shiwa/ʃíwə́ (self-name of speakers bèʃíwə́), also written chiwa (Dougère 2007), ʃiwə (Puech 1989), 'makina'/'fang makina', Osyeba/Ossyeba; spoken around Booué, Ogooué-Ivindo, Gabon; Guthrie/Maho A803, Makaa-Njem (A80), closest to Kwasio/Ngumba; Glottolog shiw1234, no ISO code (xiw proposed 2025). Not to be confused with Puech 1990 'Upstep in a Bantu tone language' (Pholia 5), which is on li-Duma/li-Wanji (B50) and was saved in the folder only because of a citation ambiguity (flagged).

sources.locator: Part 'Phonétique et phonologie', ch.3 'Système tonal', p.145 (opening) and §3.4 'Conclusion', p.174
sources.note: Part 'Phonétique et phonologie' pp.81-180; ch.3 'Système tonal' pp.145-174 treats Shiwa as a tone language (six phonetic tone realisations on three registers; four tonemes H, L, rising, falling, contour tones distinctive only on monosyllables). No section, term or statement on word accent/stress anywhere in the thesis (a full-text search for stress/accent: 'accent' occurs only in unrelated senses and in a bibliography title). Only positional remark is tonal-register: in polysyllabic lexemes initial position raises and final position lowers tone realisation (p.174).

Contains only a general remark (p.180) that in B50 'and more generally in West Bantu languages' the radical (stem-initial) vowel is stressed; not a Shiwa-specific statement.

sources.note: Ch.2 §5 'Tons' pp.79-85: tone only (H, B, plus M and extra-low B+ as word-final lowered realisations; two contour tones), nominal prefixes always L. No accent rule; the single accent remark is pp.48-49: mid-open vowels in V2 centralise, and word-finally may centralise or elide 'quand la voyelle est dénuée d'accent et donc située dans une position faible' — i.e. non-initial stem vowels are treated as unaccented/weak, with no positive statement of where accent falls.

sources.note: Image-only scan, scanned (tesseract fra, 300 dpi; saved). Deals with stem-initial onsets, C1VC2V stem shape, open-syllable structure, nasal vowels and a glottalised vocoid analysed via a 'constituant suprasyllabique'; tones marked H/B; the prenasal 'ne porte pas de ton'. Nothing on stress or accent.
